opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's interesting to look back on both, because they felt really different at the time even though on paper they're kind of the same idea: you take one language and turn it into another.

In high school, building a translator was mostly driven by curiosity. I didn't really know the theory. I didn't know what a grammar was in the formal sense, or how people usually structure a parser. I was just hacking: reading some code, trying things, getting it to work for the cases I cared about. It was fun, but it was also kind of fragile. If you threw something unexpected at it, it would probably fall apart. And honestly I didn't fully understand *why* it worked when it did work.

The compiler assignment in the ACM class was the first time I had to do it properly. You go through the whole pipeline: lexing, parsing, building an abstract syntax tree, semantic checking, an intermediate representation, and then code generation and some optimization. It's a big project, and you can't just patch your way through it, because each stage depends on the previous one being clean. So you're forced to think about abstractions. What's the right representation at each level? How do you make it easy to add a new pass or fix a bug without breaking everything else?

I think that was the real difference for me. High school taught me that I *could* build something like that, and that it was exciting. The ACM class taught me how to build it in a principled way, and how to think in terms of layers and representations. Looking back, that second lesson turned out to matter a lot later. When we started working on things like TVM, which is a compiler for machine learning, a lot of that thinking came back: what's the right intermediate representation, how do you separate what you want to compute from how you compute it, how do you make the system extensible.

So I'd say the high-school translator was where the interest started, and the compiler course was where that interest turned into an actual way of thinking about systems.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, the two experiences felt very different, even though on paper they were both "write something that takes a program and turns it into something else."

The high-school translator was really just me being curious. There was no spec, no deadline, no grading. I'd read a bit about how parsers worked and I wanted to see if I could make text go in one side and come out the other in a different form. I had no idea what a proper grammar was, no idea about intermediate representations. I just hacked on it until it worked on the examples I cared about, and then I moved on. That kind of project teaches you that you can build things that seem magical, but it doesn't really teach you how to build them well.

The ACM class compiler assignment was the opposite. You're given a real language subset, you have to handle all the cases, and your output has to actually run correctly on a test suite you don't fully control. Suddenly you can't just get the happy path working. You have to think about the structure: how the frontend hands things to the middle, how you represent the program so that optimizations are even possible, how you generate code that's correct first and fast second. And you're doing this with very strong classmates around you, so you see very quickly when your design choices are worse than someone else's.

What I think the earlier experience gave me was confidence and intuition. I wasn't scared of the problem. What the ACM project gave me was discipline and the realization that a compiler is really a system, not a trick. Looking back, a lot of how I think about TVM comes from that second lesson: you need clean abstractions between layers, because otherwise every new target or every new optimization becomes a rewrite. The high-school version would have fallen apart the moment I tried to add a second backend.

In high school, the excitement was taking something in one form and making it work in another. A compiler assignment pushes you to think about the stages involved—how you understand the input, represent it internally, and produce the output. So the connection is that same excitement about building something, but with a more structured way of thinking about it.

sol-6.1.text:
They were quite different experiences. In high school, I was mainly trying to get something working. Building a translator was exciting because I could take an idea and make the computer do something, but my approach was fairly ad hoc. I didn’t have a systematic understanding of how a compiler should be organized.

The compiler assignment in the ACM class gave me that structure. I could connect the practical problems I’d encountered with concepts like parsing, intermediate representations, and code generation. So there was a sense of revisiting something familiar, but understanding it much more deeply. The high-school project gave me the curiosity; the class helped me turn that curiosity into a more systematic way of building things.
